extracted.intended_audience: employers, occupational safety professionals, OSHA stakeholders, and policymakers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for workplace interventions to prevent heat-related illness (HRI), focusing on rest breaks, shade, fans, and hydration, and the physiological and environmental metrics used to assess effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effectiveness of rest breaks
rubrics_metrics.description: Rest breaks reduce the risk of HRI by modulating increases in heat and cardiovascular strain; studies show rest breaks result in lower core or rectal temperatures during rest periods and lower rectal temperatures over study periods, with longer breaks more effective than shorter ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA preliminarily finds rest breaks effective in reducing HRI risk. Evidence includes observational and experimental studies (e.g., Horn et al., Smallcombe et al., Meade et al., Lamarche et al.) showing lower core/rectal temperature and reduced heart rate during/after rest. Note limitations: many studies involved young, healthy, mostly male participants and short durations, which may limit generalizability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provision of shade
rubrics_metrics.description: Working or resting in shade reduces the risk of HRI by decreasing exposure to solar radiation and thereby reducing overall heat load; experimental and observational studies show shade lowers skin temperature and can improve work capacity relative to full sun.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA preliminarily finds resting in shade will reduce HRI risk. Evidence includes cycling and walking trials and observational studies showing higher skin/core/thermal sensations in sun versus shade. Effect magnitude varies by type of shade (trees, canopies, buildings), percent shade cover, time of day, season, ground cover, and microclimatic context. Limitations: many studies assessed exercise (not rest), used young/healthy participants, short durations, and some used artificial solar sources that don't mimic sun position/intensity variation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shade reduces radiant heat (microclimate measures)
rubrics_metrics.description: Shade measurably reduces radiant heat as recorded by metrics such as black globe temperature, mean radiant temperature, and thermal stress indices (e.g., Universal Thermal Climate Index).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observed reductions vary by local conditions: study-reported black globe decreases ranged ~2°C to 9°C (Fournel et al. average 4.4°C), trees decreased afternoon mean radiant temperature by up to 33.4°C in one study, and shaded areas showed substantially lower globe temperatures compared to sun (examples: beach full sun 40.9°C vs dense trees 28.9°C). Use of these microclimatic metrics can quantify shade effectiveness; expect variability by site and shade type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fans as engineering controls (general principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fans increase air movement across the skin and can increase sweat evaporation and heat loss under appropriate environmental conditions, reducing heat strain during work or rest in many working-age adults.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA preliminarily finds fans effective in reducing heat strain in the majority of working-age adults. Evidence includes chamber and field-mimicking trials showing lower rectal temperatures, skin temperatures, heart rates, and increased time to exhaustion with higher air velocities or fanning, but effects depend on ambient temperature, humidity, clothing, and whether rest occurs in cooler areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits and conditions where fans can be harmful
rubrics_metrics.description: Fans may be ineffective or harmful under certain combinations of high temperature and humidity; benefits can reverse (increase core temperature or cardiovascular strain) depending on ambient conditions, clothing, age, and medication status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical and modeling studies indicate fans can be detrimental at high temperatures/humidities (e.g., above certain humidity-dependent temperature thresholds). Some studies found fans increased core temperature or heart rate in older adults or under very hot/dry conditions. Take account of clothing (high coverage reduces benefit), rest area temperature (fans may not add benefit if rest area <24°C), and population factors like age and sweat capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fan temperature/humidity thresholds (Morris et al. model)
rubrics_metrics.description: Model-based recommended maximum ambient temperatures for fan use vary by population: 39.0°C (102.2°F) for healthy young adults, 38.0°C (100.4°F) for healthy older adults (>65), and 37.0°C (98.6°F) for older adults on anticholinergic medications (thresholds are humidity-dependent in full model).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These simplified thresholds assume a fan producing 3.5–4.5 m/s at 1 meter and use heat-balance equations; limitations include assumptions about fan speed/placement and simplified models that do not fully account for individual factors (sex, hydration, acclimatization, clothing). Use caution applying these simplified rules directly to workers without considering context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fan effectiveness classification (Foster et al. work-capacity model)
rubrics_metrics.description: Categorization of fan impact on work capacity relative to no-fan: 'beneficial' if >5% increase, 'detrimental' if >5% decrease, and 'ineffective' if change is within ±5%.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foster et al.'s trials and biophysical model found fans beneficial or ineffective at 35–40°C depending on humidity, ineffective at 45°C for higher clothing coverage, and potentially detrimental at some lower temperatures when clothing is minimal and humidity is low. Model validation and assumptions (sweat rate, fan speed) should be considered when applying classifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interaction of fans with skin wetting and fan speed (modeling evidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Models suggest that combining fans with skin wetting (e.g., misting) is more beneficial than fans alone and that fan speed influences the direction and magnitude of core temperature change across temperature/humidity combinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meade et al. modeled core temperature changes and showed that strong fans (3.5–4.5 m/s) could increase core temperature at certain humidities and temps, while slower fans (1 m/s) had different effects; combining fans with skin wetting was predicted to be beneficial or neutral in many scenarios up to 40°C. Models often assume rest rather than work and have limits when generalized to working populations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consensus/recommendation threshold for electric fans (Morrissey et al.)
rubrics_metrics.description: A consensus statement recommends electric fan use in occupational settings when ambient temperatures are below 40°C (104°F).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides a simple operational threshold used by some occupational experts, but should be applied alongside humidity, clothing, and population vulnerability considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hydration interventions (volume, timing, electrolyte use)
rubrics_metrics.description: Replacing fluids lost as sweat is necessary for cardiovascular function and thermoregulation; interventions vary in quantity, timing, and electrolyte supplementation (e.g., Ioannou et al. advised 750 mL water plus one tablespoon salt per hour).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experimental trials (e.g., McLellan and Selkirk) show that two-thirds or full fluid replacement during work/rest periods increased tolerated exposure and work time. Hydration interventions reduced prevalence of dehydration in field interventions, and electrolyte supplementation was used in some trials. Limitations: some field trials used BAU controls with unclear differences and did not measure consumed quantities directly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public hydration guidance (NIOSH/recommended rates)
rubrics_metrics.description: Public health guidance often recommends consuming ~1 cup (237 mL) every 15–20 minutes or approximately 1 liter per hour to replenish sweat losses and avoid substantial body water loss.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sweat rates vary substantially (example range 100 mL to 1 L/hr in controlled trials). Employers/policy should consider task metabolic rate, environmental conditions, and individual variability when implementing hydration schedules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hydration reduces syncope/orthostatic intolerance
rubrics_metrics.description: Drinking larger volumes of water prior to orthostatic challenge improves orthostatic tolerance (time to presyncope), increases mean blood pressure, peripheral resistance, and blunts heart rate increases; cold water can further affect cardiovascular responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studies (Schroeder et al., Parsons et al.) indicate hydration (500 mL vs 50 mL) improved orthostatic tolerance in healthy volunteers; cold water had additional hemodynamic effects. These studies were not conducted in high-heat exposure settings but are relevant given heat-related syncope mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heat-strain and performance outcome metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Key physiological and performance metrics used to evaluate interventions include core/rectal/esophageal temperature, heart rate, skin temperature, thermal sensation, time-to-exhaustion/work capacity/power output, oxygen consumption, sweat rate, heat storage, mean body temperature, and incidence/prevalence of HRI symptoms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These metrics were reported across the literature and should be used to assess intervention effectiveness. Different studies emphasize different metrics (e.g., core temperature vs. skin temperature vs. work output); interpret results considering study design (exercise vs rest), measurement methods, and population characteristics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations and generalizability of evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Many studies involve young, healthy, mostly male participants, short exposure durations, artificial solar radiation, or controlled chamber conditions that may not reflect real-world worker populations, longer shifts, or diurnal variation in solar radiation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA notes these limitations when drawing conclusions; applicability to broader workforce (older workers, females, chronic conditions, varied clothing, real work tasks) may be limited. Observational studies sometimes lack control for confounding; modeling studies rely on assumptions about fan speed, placement, sweat rates, and resting vs working states.
